overview: This map record follows Japan from 1783 to 1878, crossing a major political break. Tokugawa shoguns governed alongside regional domain lords until the Meiji Restoration of 1868. The new imperial government centralized power while schools, medicine and communications changed. Neither boundary of this map interval marks the beginning or disappearance of Japan.

periods.title: Late Tokugawa society
periods.summary: Regional domains, commercial towns and established schools formed the setting for later reforms.

periods.title: Treaties and political crisis
periods.summary: Foreign pressure and disputes among Japanese leaders weakened the shogunate.

periods.title: The first Meiji decade
periods.summary: Civil war accompanied the Restoration; new prefectures, schools and public services followed.

items.text: The Restoration was followed by fighting, not an instant peaceful handover. The Boshin War continued into 1869. In 1871 the government abolished the domains and replaced them with prefectures whose governors it appointed. A regional lord’s territory was becoming part of a centrally administered state.

Family rules changed too. In 1871 decrees permitted marriages across the former divisions between samurai, aristocrats and commoners. The same year’s Emancipation Edict abolished official outcaste status. These were changes to legal categories; issuing an edict alone could not erase people’s prejudices.

The map holds one northern outline for 1815 to 1878, but borders changed during that span. In the 1875 treaty with Russia, Japan surrendered its rights in Sakhalin in exchange for eighteen Russian-held Kuril islands. The outline should not be read as a precise treaty map for every selected year.

The Tenmei famine devastated Tsugaru in northern Honshu in 1783 to 1784, driving people away in search of survival. Later memorials preserve a community response: twelve of the monuments studied by historian Sekine Tatsuhito were erected jointly by groups of two to ten villages to remember the dead.

An 1854 print helps document year-end preparations for mochi, pounded rice cakes. The National Diet Library explains that ordinary customers ordered from sweet shops while samurai and wealthy merchant households pounded their own. Buying a festive treat and making it at home were both part of the story.

Some late Edo mochi sellers also supplied the entertainment. Morisada manko describes a performer chanting while swinging his mallet and tossing round pieces into a dish from a distance. Snack preparation could come with an acrobatic show. The Library also preserves an 1861 theatre print of mochi-pounding vendors.

Public bathing became a target of new rules. Tokyo prohibited mixed bathing in 1869, but the order had to be issued repeatedly because people did not consistently obey. Even the bathhouse reveals how a government’s preferred version of daily life could differ from actual habits.

In 1858 doctors trained in Dutch medicine pooled money to establish a vaccination center in Edo. A fire destroyed its building that same year, but work continued at other locations, including physician Ito Genboku’s residence. Medical care depended on people and cooperation as well as a permanent hospital building.

That vaccination institution became part of the shogunate’s administration in 1860 and taught Western medicine, anatomy through autopsy, and vaccination by 1861. After further reorganizations it became the University of Tokyo’s medical faculty in 1877. Its history connects late Tokugawa medical learning with early Meiji university education.

During the 1858 cholera epidemic, physician Ogata Koan translated foreign accounts and assembled a book about the disease. The outbreak spread through port cities and reached Edo. Translating knowledge was urgent practical work for doctors confronting an illness that frightened families across the country.

A print responding to cholera in the 1850s stages a battle between vegetables and fish, with the vegetables winning. The Library relates this to an Edo market panic in which fish sales collapsed and vegetable prices rose. The picture records people’s beliefs and anxieties, rather than a reliable rule for preventing disease.

sections.title: Children, schools and a written voice

items.text: National school reform did not immediately put every child behind a desk. In 1873 the recorded primary-school enrollment rate was 39.9 percent for boys and 15.1 percent for girls. These figures count children enrolled, not how often they attended, and show a large gap between the promise of schooling and access.

Kyoto’s prefectural school opened in 1872 to teach girls English, sewing and handicrafts. In 1875 it added abacus work, arithmetic and calligraphy. Its changing timetable placed practical textile skills beside language and calculation: a school day could include both a needle and an abacus.

A different experiment in Tokyo illustrates how small and fragile new opportunities could be. The government girls’ school recorded only 38 pupils in 1873 and was discontinued in 1877. Girls’ education developed through multiple local and private efforts, rather than one uninterrupted expansion of a single school.

Here is an attested Japanese book title: 学問のすゝめ, Gakumon no susume, meaning “An Encouragement of Learning.” Keio University reproduces this spelling for Fukuzawa Yukichi’s work, first issued in 1872 and expanded to seventeen pamphlets by 1876. The first installment addressed people establishing a school in his hometown of Nakatsu.

sections.title: New ways to count days and cross distances

items.text: Japan’s calendar reform made for an exceptionally short December. After the old calendar’s December 2 came January 1, 1873, under the Gregorian system. The abrupt change caused confusion, and Fukuzawa published explanations. Nobody skipped a day of living, but people suddenly needed new labels for their appointments.

Modern postal routes linked Tokyo with Kyoto and Osaka in 1871. A nationwide network followed in 1872, then flat-rate postage and postcards in 1873. A brief family message could use a standard postal service instead of depending entirely on the arrangements available along a particular journey.

Post offices soon handled more than words. Postal money orders and savings services began in 1875, alongside international mail. Sending money and setting some aside became part of the institution’s work too: the post office was becoming a place for household finances as well as letters.

The railway between Shimbashi and Yokohama opened in October 1872. Artists made woodblock prints of stations and trains around the opening, giving this new machinery a place in an established visual art. A steam train could therefore travel across a printed sheet as well as along its tracks.

ending.text: The shogunate ended in the 1868 Restoration, while Japan’s people and many institutions continued through the upheaval. The imperial government survived subsequent rebellions, including the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877. The map’s 1878 cutoff is a change of atlas record, not the end of the Meiji state.
